prompt: Naive String Matching complexity, in terms of text length n and pattern length m?
explanation: The outer loop tries n − m + 1 shifts; the inner loop compares up to m characters per shift, with no information carried over between shifts.

prompt: What is the core idea behind the Rabin-Karp algorithm?
options: Compare a numeric fingerprint (hash) of each text window against the pattern's fingerprint, instead of comparing characters.
Precompute a finite automaton that reads the text in a single pass.
Sort the text and pattern, then binary search.
Use a suffix tree of the text.
explanation: Treating P and every length-m window of T as base-d numbers lets Rabin-Karp compare O(1) numeric fingerprints instead of O(m) character comparisons.

prompt: In Rabin-Karp, if t_sft ≡ p (mod q), what can you conclude?
options: sft MIGHT be a valid shift — a spurious hit is possible, so an explicit character check is required.
sft is definitely a valid shift, no further check needed.
sft is definitely NOT a valid shift.
The algorithm has failed and must restart.
explanation: The modular test can produce false positives ('spurious hits' / 'unechte Treffer') but never false negatives. A matching hash requires an explicit character-by-character verification.

prompt: Why does Rabin-Karp compute p and t_sft modulo a prime q instead of using their exact values?
acceptedAnswers: to keep the numbers small enough to fit in a machine word
the numbers get too large otherwise
to avoid numbers larger than a computer word
explanation: For long patterns, the exact numeric values can exceed a machine word, breaking the assumption that each arithmetic operation is O(1). q is chosen so 10q still fits in a word.

prompt: What does automaton state st mean in FSM-based string matching, after reading a prefix of T?
options: The last st characters read equal P[0..st-1] (a prefix of P), and no larger overlap holds.
st counts how many total characters have been read so far.
st is always equal to the current shift sft.
st is the number of mismatches seen so far.
explanation: State st = length of the longest suffix of what's been read so far that is also a prefix of P — this can even decrease on a mismatch, unlike a naive match-counter that just resets to 0.

prompt: Which algorithm achieves O(n) matching time (after preprocessing), with no possibility of spurious hits or backtracking?
options: Finite-Automaton matching
Naive String Matching
Rabin-Karp (worst case)
None of the three guarantee O(n)
explanation: FSM matching reads T in a single O(n) pass with no backtracking after O(m·|Σ|) preprocessing — strictly better than Rabin-Karp's expected (not worst-case) O(n+m), and with no spurious hits since the automaton's transitions are exact.

prompt: [Lecture example] Run Naive String Matching with T = [a,a,b,a,a,a,a,a,b] and P = [a,a,b]. What is the list of valid shifts?
explanation: T[0..2] = 'aab' matches P directly. T[6..8] = 'aab' also matches. All other shifts fail on the first or second character comparison.

prompt: [Lecture example] Run Rabin-Karp with T = [2,1,3,1,4,9,1,3,2,3,1,4,5,3,1,4], P = [3,1,4], q = 13. What is the list of valid (real, non-spurious) shifts?
explanation: The fast modular test also passes at sft=6 and sft=10, but those are spurious hits (fail the explicit character check) — the real matches are sft = 2, 9, 13.

prompt: All three string-matching algorithms (Naive, Rabin-Karp, FSM) solve the same problem. What is the axis they actually differ on?
options: The tradeoff between preprocessing cost and per-character matching cost.
They find different sets of valid shifts.
Only some of them support patterns longer than the text.
They require different definitions of 'valid shift'.
explanation: All three return the exact same set of valid shifts for a given T and P — they differ purely in how much work is front-loaded into preprocessing versus spent per character during the scan.

prompt: [Lecture example] FSM matching with pattern P = [lambda,delta,lambda,sigma] (m=4, alphabet of 4 Greek letters) is run over a 16-character text. The automaton reaches state 4 at text index sft=12. What is the resulting valid shift?
